entry: American economist and the first American to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, awarded in 1970. His textbook *Economics: An Introductory Analysis*, first published in 1948, was the second American text to explain the principles of Keynesian economics and became the best-selling economics textbook of all time. Samuelson considered [[Mathematics|mathematics]] the natural language of economists, and his *Foundations of Economic Analysis* contributed to the mathematical foundations of the field. He advised President [[John F. Kennedy]] and President [[Lyndon B. Johnson]], and joined the faculty of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1940. With [[Milton Friedman]] he wrote a weekly column for *Newsweek* representing opposing views; Samuelson called himself a "Cafeteria Keynesian" who accepted only what he found good in Keynesianism.

American singer-songwriter and guitarist. Half of [[Simon & Garfunkel]], the 1960s folk-rock duo, he later recorded solo albums drawing on gospel, reggae and soul. His 1986 album *Graceland*, which incorporated South African influences, was his most successful and acclaimed, and produced "You Can Call Me Al." He has won 16 [[Grammy Awards]] and was twice inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]. He hosted [[Saturday Night Live]] four times between 1975 and 1987.

American filmmaker known for psychological dramas about dysfunctional families, alienation, loneliness and redemption, shot with constantly moving cameras and long takes. His films include *Boogie Nights* (1997), *Magnolia* (1999) and *There Will Be Blood* (2007). *One Battle After Another* (2025) earned him Academy Awards for Best Picture and Best Director, and he has won three [[Academy Awards]] in all. He is the only person to have won the Academy Award for Best Director and directorial prizes at Europe's three major film festivals, including [[Cannes Film Festival|Cannes]].

Christian apostle and missionary, originally named Saul of Tarsus. Paul was not one of the Twelve Apostles, but after a vision on the road to [[Damascus]] he was baptized and began proclaiming that [[Jesus]] was the Jewish messiah and the Son of God. He made three missionary journeys to spread the Christian message among non-Jewish communities, founding churches in Asia Minor and Europe from the mid-40s to the mid-50s AD. Fourteen of the 27 books of the [[New Testament]] have traditionally been attributed to him, and seven of his epistles are undisputed by scholars. Christians have read Paul as saying that people are saved through faith rather than by following Jewish law. He argued with other early leaders over the circumcision of Gentiles.

German field marshal and statesman, president of Germany from 1925 to 1934. He led the Imperial German Army in World War I. Recalled from retirement in 1914, he won the Battle of Tannenberg on the [[Eastern Front (World War I)|Eastern Front]] and became a national hero. In 1916 he replaced Erich von Falkenhayn as Chief of the General Staff, and with [[Erich Ludendorff]] he established a de facto military dictatorship. Elected president of the [[Weimar Republic]] in 1925, he was opposed to [[Adolf Hitler]] and the [[Nazi Party]], yet in January 1933 he appointed Hitler chancellor in a coalition government. He signed the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act of 1933, which gave the Nazi regime emergency powers. After Hindenburg's death the following year, Hitler combined the presidency with the chancellery and declared himself Führer ('leader').

Quantum mechanics principle barring identical fermions from sharing a quantum state. Formulated by Austrian physicist [[Wolfgang Pauli]] in 1925 for electrons, and extended to all fermions through his spin–statistics theorem of 1940, it holds that identical particles with half-integer spin cannot occupy the same quantum state. For electrons in an atom, no two can have the same values of all four quantum numbers: principal, azimuthal, magnetic and spin. This restriction explains how electron shells fill and underlies the structure of the [[Periodic table]], which limits each orbital to two electrons with opposite spins. It also underpins the stability of everyday matter. Bosons, particles with integer spin such as [[Photon|photons]], are not subject to the principle.

Set of three 2×2 complex matrices used in quantum mechanics. Named after physicist [[Wolfgang Pauli]], they are traceless, Hermitian, involutory and unitary, and are usually denoted by σ (sigma). They occur in the Pauli equation, which describes the interaction of a particle's [[Spin (physics)|spin]] with an electromagnetic field. Together with the identity matrix, they form a basis for all 2×2 Hermitian matrices over the real numbers. Their multiples by i generate transformations in the sense of Lie algebras.

American multinational financial technology company that operates an online payments system in most countries that support online money transfers. It serves as an electronic alternative to checks and money orders and processes payments for online vendors and auction sites for a fee. PayPal was formed in March 2000 by a merger of Confinity and X.com, which [[Elon Musk]] had founded. It went public in 2002, and [[EBay|eBay]] acquired it later that year for $1.5 billion. eBay spun it off as an independent company in 2015. PayPal ranked 143rd on the 2022 Fortune 500.

American professional golfer who won 11 PGA Tour events, including three major championships. He won the 1989 PGA Championship and the 1991 U.S. Open after a playoff against Scott Simpson. At the 1999 U.S. Open at Pinehurst, he holed a 15-foot (5 m) par putt on the final hole for a one-stroke victory over Phil Mickelson. Stewart was known for his fluid swing and for ivy caps and plus-four-style knickers, a throwback to the golf uniform of an earlier era. His last major came a few months before his death in an airplane accident.

Flowering plant whose seeds and pods are eaten as a vegetable, *Pisum sativum*. Native to the Mediterranean region and southwest Asia, the pea is an annual, cool-season crop now cultivated nearly worldwide. [[Carl Linnaeus]] gave it its scientific name in 1753, meaning cultivated pea; some sources now classify it as *Lathyrus oleraceus*, a change that is disputed. Botanically, pea pods are fruit. Immature peas are eaten fresh, frozen or canned, while field peas are grown to produce dried peas, the basis of pease porridge and pea soup, staples of medieval cuisine. Pea plants can self-pollinate. Its large genome made the pea difficult to sequence; a draft reference genome was announced in September 2019.

Two treaties signed in October 1648 at Osnabrück and Münster, ending the [[Thirty Years' War]] in the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. The war killed between 4.5 and 8 million people. Emperor Ferdinand III, France, Sweden and their allies took part, and 109 delegations attended, though not all at the same time. The two cities were chosen because each side wanted to meet on territory under its own control. A separate treaty ending the [[Eighty Years' War]] between Spain and the Dutch Republic was signed in Münster on 30 January 1648. Several scholars of [[International relations|international relations]] regard the treaties as the origin of Westphalian sovereignty, but some historians argue such views emerged in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

Deciduous fruit tree of the rose family, or its fruit. *Prunus persica* was first domesticated and cultivated in [[China]] during the [[Neolithic|Neolithic period]]. The specific name refers to its cultivation in Persia (modern-day Iran), from where it was transplanted to Europe. The tree is relatively short lived, usually not exceeding twenty years of age, and is typically about 3 m (10 ft) tall. Nectarines are smooth-skinned peaches of the same species. In 2023 China produced 65% of the world total of peaches and nectarines, and no other leading country produced more than 5%. The fruit is regarded as a symbol of longevity in China.

Group of three pheasant-family birds in the genera *Pavo* and *Afropavo*. Males, called peacocks, display an elaborate train of eyespotted upper tail coverts in courtship, while females, called peahens, are drab. The blue or Indian peafowl is native to the [[Indian subcontinent]]. The green peafowl lives in Southeast Asia, and the Congo peafowl is native only to the Congo Basin. The peacock's colors are structural rather than pigmented, produced by light reflected from regular nanostructures in the feathers. [[Charles Darwin]] suggested that the train evolved through sexual selection to attract females. Amotz Zahavi's handicap principle proposed instead that such features are honest signals of fitness.

Legume cultivated as a grain and oil crop, *Arachis hypogaea*, also called the groundnut. Native to South America, where cultivated peanuts arose from a hybrid of two wild species, it fruits underground. After fertilization a stalk called a peg grows into the soil and forms the pod, a feature called geocarpy that led [[Carl Linnaeus]] to name the species *hypogaea*, from Greek for 'under the earth'. Like other legumes, peanuts host nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules that improve soil fertility. Peanuts are used for oil, peanut butter and sauces, and oilcake meal serves as animal feed and fertilizer. Some people are allergic to peanuts and can have a fatal reaction.

Syndicated daily and Sunday American comic strip written and illustrated by [[Charles M. Schulz]]. It ran from October 2, 1950, to February 13, 2000, and at Schulz's death appeared in over 2,600 newspapers, with a readership of about 355 million in 75 countries. Schulz drew all 17,897 strips without assistants, and the strip was translated into 21 languages. Its main character, Charlie Brown, is meek and lacks self-confidence, and his friend Lucy Van Pelt always pulls away the football he tries to kick. The cast includes the beagle [[Snoopy]]. The franchise includes five animated theatrical films and television specials such as *A Charlie Brown Christmas*. The title was imposed by the syndicate, and Schulz disliked it.

Edible pome fruit of trees in the genus *Pyrus*, family [[Rosaceae]]. Pear trees are mostly small or medium-sized and native to Asia, distributed across Europe and the mountains of North Africa. About 3,000 varieties are grown worldwide, varying in shape and taste. In 2024 world production was about 28 million tonnes, led by [[China]] with 76% of the total. The fruit is eaten fresh, canned, dried, as juice, or fermented as perry. Pears were cultivated in China as early as 2000 BC. The wood is a preferred material for high-quality [[Woodwind instrument|woodwind instruments]] and furniture. Like [[Apple|apples]], pears are pomes; the edible flesh is a swollen receptacle that encloses the true fruit, the core.

Hard, shiny object produced within the mantle of a living shelled mollusk. Pearls are composed of [[Calcium carbonate|calcium carbonate]], mainly aragonite, deposited in concentric layers. Natural pearls form without human intervention and are very rare, so most pearls sold are cultured or farmed from [[Oyster|pearl oysters]] and freshwater mussels. Gem-quality pearls are nacreous and iridescent, and their luster depends on light reflected from thin, numerous layers. Pearls can be dyed, and the most valuable have a metallic, highly reflective luster. Because they are made largely of calcium carbonate, they dissolve in vinegar. Most shelled mollusks can produce some kind of pearl, but most have no value except as curiosities.

American rock band from [[Seattle]], Washington, formed in 1990 and one of the key bands of the grunge movement. Its members have been guitarists Stone Gossard and Mike McCready, bassist Jeff Ament and vocalist Eddie Vedder since its formation. The debut album *Ten* (1991) stayed on the Billboard 200 for nearly five years and was certified 13× platinum. In 1994 the band unsuccessfully sued Ticketmaster, claiming it monopolized the concert-ticket market. Pearl Jam was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2017, in its first year of eligibility, and has sold more than 100 million albums worldwide.

Major river system in southern China, formed by the Xi, Bei and Dong rivers, which flow into the South China Sea through the Pearl River Delta. The system is China's third-longest river, after the [[Yangtze]] and the [[Yellow River]], and its second largest by volume, after the Yangtze. Its basin covers 453,700 sq km and drains most of [[Guangdong]] and Guangxi, parts of Yunnan, Guizhou, Hunan and Jiangxi, and the northernmost parts of Vietnam. The river flows through [[Guangzhou]], and its estuary separates [[Macau]] and Zhuhai from Hong Kong and Shenzhen. The name refers to pearl-colored shells in its riverbed at Guangzhou.

Pre-industrial agricultural laborer or farmer with limited land ownership, especially under feudalism in the Middle Ages. Peasants paid rent, tax or services to a landlord, and in Europe they were non-free slaves, semi-free [[Serfdom|serfs]] or free tenants. Peasants made up most of the agricultural labor force in pre-industrial societies; one estimate puts their share of the medieval population at 85%. Under the open field system that dominated medieval Europe, peasants lived on manors and shared common land. After the [[Black Death]] reduced the population in the mid-14th century, survivors gained more land and labor became scarcer, improving the position of peasants in Western Europe.

Uprising across large parts of England in 1381, also called Wat Tyler's Rebellion. Its causes included tensions from the [[Black Death]], high taxes for the [[Hundred Years' War]] and instability in London's local leadership. Its scale deterred later Parliaments from raising taxes to pay for campaigns in France. The revolt was once thought to have caused a promise by King Richard II to abolish serfdom, but historians are less certain of its lasting impact. Socialist writers, including William Morris, have used it as a symbol for the political left.

Accumulation of partially decayed vegetation or organic matter, formed in waterlogged wetlands. Peat forms when plant material does not fully decay in acidic, oxygen-poor conditions, and [[Sphagnum]] moss is among its most common components. It accumulates at about a millimeter a year, and its deposits preserve pollen and plant remains that record past vegetation and climate. Peatlands cover 3.7 million square kilometers and store up to 550 gigatonnes of carbon, about 42% of soil carbon, although they cover just 3% of the land's surface. Peat is often the first step in the formation of [[Coal|coal]]. Burning and draining peat have released large amounts of [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] into the atmosphere.

Species of [[Hickory]] whose seed is an edible nut. *Carya illinoinensis* is a large deciduous tree native to the south-central United States and northern Mexico, in the region of the [[Mississippi River]]. It is cultivated for its nut primarily in [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], New Mexico, [[Texas]] and [[Louisiana]], and in Mexico. The nut is eaten as a snack and used in praline candy and pecan pie. The pecan is the state nut of Alabama, Arkansas, California, Texas and Louisiana, and the state tree of Texas. Trees typically grow 20 to 40 m (66 to 131 ft) tall. The husk splits into four sections at maturity to release the thin-shelled seed.

New World family of pig-like ungulates, Tayassuidae. Peccaries, also called javelinas or skunk pigs, are found from the southwestern United States through Central and [[South America]]. Adults usually weigh 20 to 40 kg and measure 90 to 130 cm in length. They are the closest relatives of [[Pig|pigs]], though they have a non-ruminating, three-chambered stomach and short, straight tusks that interlock. Peccaries live in herds; a group that travels together is called a squadron, and averages six to nine members. They are omnivores whose preferred foods are roots, grasses, seeds, fruit and cacti, particularly prickly pear. Peccaries first appeared in North America during the [[Miocene]].

Theory and practice of teaching and of the [[Learning|learning]] process. As an academic discipline, pedagogy studies how knowledge and skills are imparted in an educational context, including the interactions between teachers and students. Its most common definition is the study of teaching methods, but some regard it as an art or craft based on tacit knowledge, and others as a catch-all term. Its aims range from liberal education, the general development of human potential, to vocational training in specific skills. Instructive strategies depend on students' background knowledge, their goals and their environment; one example is the [[Socratic method]]. Didactics is usually seen as the narrower term.
